A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CREA with the same authors, core framework and principal experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original image-generation and editing evaluations, a 50-participant user study, component ablations and qualitative applications.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds RF-Inversion comparisons, a 25-participant GenArtist study and additional qualitative demonstrations.

M1.justification: The five-agent workflow, contrastive prompt fusion, creativity scoring and iterative refinement remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 is identical apart from formatting and relocation. New system prompts document the existing procedure, while GPT-4o provides an additional backend demonstration.

E1.justification: V2 adds a scene-editing scenario involving small-object insertion, localized recoloring and broader background changes (Appendix D.4.2, Figure 18). The original creative editing, generation, personalization and video coverage remains, including the same 24-object quantitative evaluation.

E2.justification: V2 adds RF-Inversion to a quantitative editing comparison using the same Flux backbone (Table 4), and GenArtist to a human evaluation of creativity and edit disentanglement (Table 5). These address important comparator gaps. GenArtist was only discussed in v1; the original evaluated baseline sets remain.

E3.justification: V2 adds FID/KID evaluation, a matched-backbone comparison, a separate 25-participant GenArtist study and a GPT-4o image-generator configuration. The component ablation drops its LLM-creativity metric. Existing 600-image task evaluations, the 50-participant study and principal generation settings remain unchanged; Canny conditioning is newly disclosed.

E4.justification: Appendix D.3 adds a controlled comparison testing whether advantages depend on the Flux backbone. D.4 adds GPT-4o backend generalization and a fine-grained editing case study. Original parameter, refinement and negative-prompting analyses remain, but the component ablation loses its LLM-creativity assessment.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the same-seed comparison statement and plus/minus reporting for existing results. V2 introduces no repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or explicit significance tests. Its additional study uses the existing reporting style.

E6.justification: Existing Table 1 scores and the relocated LLM-judge table retain their values. V2 adds FID/KID results, RF-Inversion scores and GenArtist-study means: creativity 4.299 versus 2.893 and disentanglement 3.726 versus 2.850 for CREA versus GenArtist. It also adds qualitative demonstrations, removes the LLM-creativity ablation results and trims gallery examples. These are added or removed findings, not improvements over v1 under unchanged settings.

T1.justification: The Creativity Index definition, generation and refinement equations, and optimization objective are mathematically unchanged despite conversion to inline notation. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs. Removed creativity-theory background is conceptual rather than mathematical.

C1.justification: The central claims remain a novel collaborative framework for creative editing and generation, optional user guidance, improved creative outputs, and applicability to personalization and video. Abstract shortening and consolidation of contribution bullets do not materially change these claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for orchestration overhead, SDXL's usability advantage and the matched-backbone findings. It explicitly places definitive creativity assessment outside the paper's scope and adds labor-impact discussion, while removing the video-motion inconsistency caveat. The central interpretation of CREA's creativity and diversity benefits remains.

D1.justification: V2 supplies full agent, fusion and scoring prompts, an end-to-end editing trace, and prompts for teaser examples (Tables 6–21, Figure 11). It specifies Canny conditioning and GPU memory, and changes code availability from promised to reported public availability. However, it removes v1's QWEN2.5-VL-32B evaluation-judge specification without establishing a judge change.

R1.justification: V2 removes the substantial supplemental creativity and agent-framework surveys in v1 Appendix B and C.1–C.3, including discussion and citations for AutoGPT, CAMEL, MetaGPT and others. It adds C3 and RF-Inversion references and develops direct comparisons with prior agentic and Flux-based approaches. The central novelty positioning remains.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper, condenses the abstract and contributions, rewrites the methodology opening, and combines limitations and conclusion under Discussion. The appendix is extensively reorganized around architecture, prompts and experiments, replacing broad background sections and relocating Algorithm 1 and the LLM-judge table.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. Dialogue figures are enlarged and redistributed, qualitative galleries are shortened, and new comparison tables, prompt/log tables and demonstration figures are added. Table 1 gains FID/KID columns, while the component-ablation table loses its creativity column.

improvement.justification: Full system prompts and execution traces substantially improve reproducibility beyond v1's role descriptions and illustrative dialogue. The matched-Flux comparison and GenArtist user study address important weaknesses in the empirical comparisons. These gains outweigh the loss of the judge-model specification and creativity-ablation column, although the new FID/KID results still lack a specified reference-data protocol.
